gap: No result ChatGPT got states what a 5,000 W-class station costs per watt-hour or per minute at a 5,000 W load at today's maker-store prices: Pecron F5000LFP $0.47/Wh (pre-order, ships early January), Nature's Generator L6000 and OUPES Guardian 6000 V2 tied at $0.59/Wh, Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus $0.69/Wh.
standout_why: Compared against solarwaypoint.com and holdbackup.com (both cited), powerbencher.com and thewattguide.com. All four print no prices, so none can state cost per Wh or per watt. Runtime at 5,000 W is already covered (thewattguide: 51 min for 5,040 Wh and 39 min for 3,840 Wh; powerbencher: 46 min for the F3800; ChatGPT's own answer: 50-55 min and 38-41 min). Wh per lb is on powerbencher for the older F3800 only. None of the four lists the Nature's Generator L6000, and only thewattguide mentions the OUPES Guardian 6000 V2 and Pecron F5000LFP. The new part is the price-based figures and the comparison of the Jackery's premium with an L6000 expansion battery.
decides: It moves the value pick away from ChatGPT's Jackery pick, but it does not make the L6000 a clear #1. The Jackery ($3,499) costs 18% more per Wh than the L6000 ($2,249.99) or the OUPES Guardian 6000 V2 ($2,699); its extra 1,200 Wh over the L6000 costs $1.04/Wh, while the L6000's Power Pod adds 3,840 Wh at $0.39/Wh. L6000 + Power Pod is $3,749.98 for 7,680 Wh (about 78 min at 5,000 W), against the Jackery alone at about 51 min for $251 less. The L6000 and the OUPES tie to the cent on $/Wh and on dollars per minute at 5,000 W; the OUPES gives 768 Wh (about 8 minutes) more for $449 more, and the L6000 is the lower ticket for the same 6,000 W. The Pecron is cheapest per Wh but is a pre-order shipping early January, more than four weeks out. The L6000's standing depends on the sale price: at the $2,999.99 list price in Dealectric's record it would be $0.78/Wh, behind both the OUPES and the Jackery. I could not re-read that list price or the Nov 29 end date today.

findings.note: $2,249.99 ÷ 3,840 Wh = $0.586/Wh. Price, 'available: true', 3,840 Wh LiFePO4 and '6000W continuous' at 120/240 V come from the store's own search listing for this URL, read with storecheck.py search; the product page itself returned HTTP 429 on every attempt.

findings.label: Minutes at a 5,000 W load and dollars per minute
findings.source_title: Nature's Generator L6000 Expandable Power Station
findings.note: 3,840 Wh × 0.85 ÷ 5,000 W × 60 = 39.2 min; $2,249.99 ÷ 39.2 = $57.4. The 0.85 is an assumed usable share, not a measurement; before losses it is 46 min.

findings.label: Wall refill time from the maker's AC input watts
findings.source_title: Nature's Generator L6000 Expandable Power Station
findings.note: 3,840 ÷ 1,800 = 2.13 h; 3,840 ÷ 3,600 = 1.07 h, before charging losses. The maker states '1,800W or 3,600W AC charging' and '80% charge in approximately 1.2 hours'. Each hour at 5,000 W takes 5,000 ÷ 1,800 = 2.8 h to put back from a 120 V socket, or 1.4 h at 3,600 W.

findings.label: What 3,600 W charging needs
findings.value: Super Charging Cable, $119.99, and a 240 V NEMA 14-50R outlet
findings.source_title: Nature's Generator Lithium 6ft Super Charging Cable
findings.note: Store listing: 'Charge the L6000 to 80% in about 1.2 hours', 'Requires NEMA 14-50R Outlet'. Read with storecheck.py search.

findings.label: Wh per lb
findings.source_title: pv magazine (Ryan Kennedy, 13 Aug 2025): Nature's Generator releases compact home backup battery
findings.note: pv magazine gives 50.8 kg; × 2.2046 = 112.0 lb; 3,840 ÷ 112.0 = 34.3. The same article gives 3,000 cycles, 6 kW continuous and an L14-30R outlet. The maker's own weight could not be opened (429).

findings.label: Cost per Wh with one Power Pod
findings.note: Power Pod $1,499.99, 'adds additional 3840Wh'. ($2,249.99 + $1,499.99) ÷ 7,680 = $0.488/Wh; 7,680 × 0.85 ÷ 5,000 × 60 = 78.3 min. The Pod alone is $1,499.99 ÷ 3,840 = $0.391/Wh. That is a station plus an extra battery, so it is not a row for the unit-alone table.

findings.label: 5,000 W drain against a 120 V wall socket
findings.value: 2.8 h of charging per hour of 5,000 W use
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX F3800 Plus Portable Power Station
findings.note: 5,000 W ÷ 1,800 W = 2.78. This holds for the Anker (1,800 W max AC input) and for the L6000 on its standard cable (1,800 W, Nature's Generator listing). On 240 V at 3,600 W (L6000 with Super Charging Cable, Pecron with 30 A cable) it is 5,000 ÷ 3,600 = 1.4 h.
